# The Defence Corridor: Lockheed, SRI, and the Military Substrate {#sec-4-04}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1956–1970
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** What is Silicon Valley actually built on?

**The answer.** On military money, and for its first twenty-five years on almost
nothing else. Lockheed in Sunnyvale, SRI in Menlo Park, NASA Ames in Mountain
View: the early Valley was a defence cluster with a university attached. The
internet's first transmission went to a Stanford-adjacent laboratory on Defense
Department funding, and that is the least surprising fact in this book.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy, at a scale that dwarfs everything private in
the region for a generation. The chapter's function is corrective: it removes
the garage from the centre of the story and puts the procurement office there,
which is what Act III ch. 11 promised it would do.

**The key fact.** The first ARPANET message was sent on 29 October 1969 from
UCLA to SRI in Menlo Park. The system crashed after two letters. The internet's
first word was 'lo'.

**The human anchor.** Lockheed Missiles and Space in Sunnyvale, which by the
1960s was the largest employer in the county — a fact that the Valley's own
origin story has almost entirely forgotten.

**Excluded voices.** The public, again, through classification — and this time
the exclusion produces a response. The chapter should end pointing at ch. 7,
because the students who occupied the Applied Electronics Laboratory were
objecting to precisely what this chapter describes.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that Silicon Valley was a military-industrial
cluster before it was a consumer one by showing employment, revenue, and
research funding concentrated in defence work through 1970.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

The first message sent over the ARPANET, on 29 October 1969, went from UCLA to
SRI in Menlo Park. The system crashed after two letters, so the internet's first
word was "lo". It was sent between two Defense Department contractors on Defense
Department money, and it is the least surprising fact in this book.

The chapter's job is corrective. The garage sits at the centre of the Valley's
story about itself; the procurement office is what actually happened, and this
is where Act III's promise gets discharged. Lockheed Missiles and Space arrived
in Sunnyvale in 1956 and became the largest employer in the county — a fact the
region's origin mythology has almost entirely forgotten. SRI had been founded by
Stanford in 1946 and was still owned by the university, a detail this act's
seventh chapter turns on entirely. NASA Ames sat at Moffett Field in Mountain
View, inheriting an aeronautics establishment that predated all of it.

Follow the revenue and the picture is unambiguous. Through the 1960s the
region's major firms depended overwhelmingly on defence and aerospace contracts,
and the consumer market barely existed. Silicon Valley was a military-industrial
cluster with a university attached, and it was that for roughly twenty-five
years.

Douglas Engelbart's 1968 demonstration at SRI — the mouse, hypertext, windowed
displays, collaborative editing — was federally funded, and the interface ideas
in it reappear at Xerox PARC and then in a personal computer five chapters
later.

The exclusion here is the public, through classification. It paid for the
research and was not permitted to examine it, and the chapter names that as the
grievance it is about to become. Some of the people on that campus are beginning
to work out what their university is building, and in three chapters they will
occupy a laboratory over it.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
What is Silicon Valley actually built on?
:::

The first message sent over the ARPANET went from UCLA to the Stanford Research
Institute in Menlo Park on 29 October 1969. The sender typed L, then O, and the
system crashed.

The internet's first word was "lo".

It was sent between two Defense Department contractors, over a network the
Defense Department had commissioned, to a node at an institute owned by Stanford
University. Every element of that sentence is Act III's triangle, and this
chapter is about the twenty-five years in which the triangle, and not the
garage, was Silicon Valley.

## Lockheed

The largest employer in Santa Clara County for most of the 1960s and 1970s was
Lockheed.

Lockheed Missiles and Space Division opened in Sunnyvale in 1956, adjacent to
Moffett Field, and grew very fast on the Polaris submarine-launched ballistic
missile programme and on classified satellite reconnaissance work. Employment
reached the tens of thousands. It was, by a wide margin, the region's dominant
industrial enterprise.

Almost nobody tells the story of Silicon Valley this way, and the omission is
instructive. Lockheed made no consumer product, had one customer, and operated
substantially in secret. It employed more people in the Valley than Hewlett-
Packard and Fairchild combined for years, and it does not appear in the origin
story at all, because the origin story is about garages and Lockheed was a
procurement relationship.

## SRI

The Stanford Research Institute had been founded by the university in 1946 as a
non-profit to conduct applied research for industry and government.

The ownership relationship is worth stating precisely, because the next chapters
but three turn on it entirely: SRI was established by Stanford's trustees, and
Stanford owned it. It was located in Menlo Park, a few miles from the campus,
and it grew through the 1950s and 1960s on contract research, a substantial and
increasing proportion of it for military and intelligence agencies.

By the late 1960s that work included research on chemical and biological warfare
and on counterinsurgency techniques relevant to the war in Vietnam, and the
university's ownership of the institute doing it was a matter of public record.

## Ames, and the rest

NASA Ames Research Center sat at Moffett Field in Mountain View, inheriting an
aeronautics establishment that dated to the 1930s and adding wind tunnels,
computing, and eventually space science.

Around these anchors accumulated the suppliers: electronics firms, instrument
makers, and the semiconductor companies from the previous chapter, whose early
volume came from missile and space programmes.

Follow the revenue across the region in 1965 and the picture is unambiguous.
Defence and aerospace purchasing was the dominant source of demand. The consumer
market for electronics existed but was small and was served largely by Japanese
manufacturers. Silicon Valley was a military-industrial cluster with a
university attached, and it was that for roughly a quarter of a century.

## ARPANET

The network came out of the same arrangement and the chapter should describe it
as a procurement rather than as a revelation.

The Advanced Research Projects Agency had been created in 1958 in response to
Sputnik, and its Information Processing Techniques Office funded computing
research at universities and institutes across the country. Those installations
had incompatible machines and no way to share resources, and connecting them was
a practical problem worth money.

The first four nodes were UCLA, SRI, the University of California at Santa
Barbara, and the University of Utah. The technical approach — packet switching,
with no central control — had been developed independently by Paul Baran at RAND
in Santa Monica and Donald Davies in Britain, and the redundancy that later
proved so valuable was a design property from the start.

Baran's motivation at RAND had included survivability of communications under
nuclear attack, and the frequently repeated claim that the internet was designed
to survive a nuclear war is an overstatement of this that the people involved
have spent decades correcting. The chapter states the accurate version:
survivability was one strand in the intellectual origins of packet switching,
and the ARPANET itself was built to share expensive computers.

## Engelbart

The other thing happening at SRI in the 1960s was Douglas Engelbart's
Augmentation Research Center, and it was federally funded from the same sources.

In December 1968, at a conference in San Francisco, Engelbart gave a
demonstration that has been known ever since as the Mother of All Demos. In
ninety minutes he showed a live networked computer system with a mouse, a
windowed display, hypertext links, real-time collaborative document editing,
video conferencing, and version control. In 1968.

Almost none of it was commercialised by SRI. The people went on to Xerox PARC, a
few miles away, and Act IV chapter 9 describes what happened to it there. The
mouse patent was assigned to SRI, which licensed it to Apple years later for a
modest sum.

Federal money, a Stanford-owned institute, a working demonstration of the
interface every subsequent computer would use, and no commercial capture
whatsoever. The invention and the fortune are separated by fifteen years and two
changes of ownership, which is a pattern worth remembering when the industry
explains itself.

## What the arrangement produced

The chapter should give the arrangement its due before turning on it, because
the output was extraordinary.

Satellite reconnaissance, developed in secret at Lockheed and elsewhere, gave
the United States and eventually the Soviet Union the ability to verify what the
other side actually had — which made arms control agreements possible and
removed a category of catastrophic misjudgment. The Corona programme's imagery
established in the early 1960s that the missile gap the 1960 election had been
fought over did not exist.

Integrated circuits reached volume production because missile and space
programmes bought them at any price. Computing, satellite navigation, digital
signal processing, and the network itself all came out of the same channel.

None of this would have been funded by a private market on the timescales
involved, because the returns were decades away and unappropriable. The case for
the arrangement is strong, and Act V's chapters on AI infrastructure will have
occasion to remember it.

The chapter's argument is not that public research funding is a mistake. It is
that this particular arrangement routed the benefits in a specific direction,
and the direction was not chosen by anyone who could be voted out.

## The grievance forming

The public paid for all of this and could not look at most of it.

Classification covered the Lockheed work almost entirely, a growing share of
SRI's contracts, and a substantial fraction of Stanford's own engineering
research, including the Applied Electronics Laboratory, which by the late 1960s
was the campus centre of classified work.

There was also a specific local grievance about land. Stanford had leased large
tracts of the industrial park to defence contractors, and the university's
research budget had come to depend substantially on classified contracts. The
institution that had been endowed to serve the children of California was, by
the late 1960s, deriving a significant part of its income from work its own
students were not permitted to read.

Terman and his generation regarded this as unremarkable — wartime practice
continued into a cold war that showed no sign of ending. But the arrangement had
a constituency it had not consulted, and that constituency was living on the
campus in increasing numbers and had begun reading the budget.

In April 1969 several hundred of them walked into the Applied Electronics
Laboratory and shut it down, and chapter 7 is what happened next.
